article.title: Socialism Matters
article.author: Peter McLaren
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. As the midterms loom, the question of socialism becomes increasingly urgent. We are told that we live in democracies. We vote, debate, protest, and occasionally celebrate the spectacle of our collective sovereignty. Yet for most working people, democracy stops at the factory gate, the office door, the hospital corridor, and the university's administrative suite. The decisions that shape our working lives remain concentrated in the hands of owners, executives, shareholders, and managerial elites. We are invited to govern ourselves as citizens while being governed by others as workers. Here lies capitalism's great democratic contradiction: political equality is proclaimed in public while economic subordination is normalized in everyday life. Socialism matters because it asks whether democracy can remain meaningful while the economic institutions governing our lives are organized around private power. It is not simply a question of redistributing wealth after it has been accumulated, nor of asking the state to soften capitalism's cruelties. It is a question of transforming the social relations through which wealth is produced, controlled, and distributed. It asks who decides what society produces, whose needs production serves, who performs the work, and who appropriates the surplus generated by collective labor. I want to approach this question through two concepts that have become important to my own critical vocabulary: mausolocracy and ensepulcher. These terms are not decorative additions to a critique of capitalism. They are intended to perform analytical work. By mausolocracy, I mean a political-economic order in which accumulated capital and entrenched power are monumentalized, protected, and reproduced as if they were permanent features of human existence. The term evokes a mausoleum because capitalism does more than concentrate wealth: it builds institutions, laws, ideologies, and cultural arrangements that preserve the power of the living at the expense of possibilities for the living. Its monuments are not only the skyscrapers of finance, the gated enclaves of the wealthy, or the corporate empires that tower over public life. They are also the institutions that teach us to regard private ownership of productive resources as natural, economic hierarchy as inevitable, and the subordination of human needs to profitability as common sense. Mausolocracy names the architecture of this power: the institutionalized arrangements through which capital secures its authority across economic, political, cultural, and educational life. It helps explain why formal political democracy can coexist with profound economic inequality, why governments can remain responsive to concentrated wealth while claiming to represent the public, and why the accumulation of private power so often appears more politically consequential than the needs of ordinary people. Ensepulcher, by contrast, names the active process through which emancipatory alternatives are buried. If mausolocracy is the architecture of entrenched power, ensepulcher is the work required to keep that architecture standing. It operates materially, institutionally, and ideologically. It buries alternatives beneath the assertion that there is no viable alternative; it converts historically produced inequalities into apparent facts of nature; it teaches people to imagine themselves as competitors in a permanent struggle for individual survival rather than as participants in the collective transformation of society. It does not merely silence dissent. It seeks to make dissent appear futile before it begins. These concepts help us understand why socialism matters beyond the familiar arguments about taxation, public spending, or the size of government. The central issue is whether human beings can exercise democratic control over the institutions that organize their collective lives—or whether democracy will remain subordinate to the imperatives of capital. Related: Elbows Up! Canada, Trump, and the Politics of Democratic Friendship FROM WORKPLACE HIERARCHY TO WORKPLACE DEMOCRACY Richard D. Wolff offers an important point of departure. In his discussion of socialism, Wolff distinguishes regulated private capitalism, state capitalism, and forms of socialism that seek to democratize the workplace. For Wolff, an economy does not become socialist simply because the state regulates private enterprise or takes ownership of productive institutions. The deeper question concerns the relations of power within the enterprise itself. An enterprise remains capitalist when employers direct workers' labor and retain exclusive authority over the surplus that labor generates. Wolff argues that a genuinely socialist enterprise must abolish the rigid distinction between employers and employees by placing production and its proceeds under collective, democratic control. This is a crucial distinction. Socialism, in this understanding, is not merely a more generous distribution of the fruits of an otherwise unchanged economic system. It involves democratizing the process through which those fruits are produced. Workers in a democratically organized enterprise would participate in decisions about what goods and services to produce; how production should be organized; which technologies to adopt; what working conditions to establish; how necessary tasks should be shared; and how the surplus generated by their collective labor should be distributed. They would deliberate over whether that surplus should support reinvestment, improve wages and working conditions, strengthen the enterprise's long-term sustainability, or advance collectively determined social priorities. These are not minor administrative questions. They concern the allocation of human time, the organization of social cooperation, and the purposes to which productive capacity is directed. They concern whether people enter the workplace as democratic participants or as subordinates required to surrender much of their agency for the duration of the working day. Wolff's argument also challenges the assumption that state ownership alone guarantees socialism. A state-owned enterprise can reproduce hierarchical relations if officials retain authority over workers and workers remain excluded from meaningful decision-making. Public ownership can matter enormously, but ownership on paper does not automatically produce democracy in practice. The decisive question is whether people gain effective collective power over the organization of production and the distribution of its results. This does not mean that workplace democracy, by itself, resolves every problem of economic coordination, ecological sustainability, or political representation. Nor does it mean that every decision can be made without expertise, delegation, or wider social planning. It means that such arrangements must themselves be democratically accountable rather than treated as excuses for preserving the power of a minority. From the perspective of mausolocracy, the significance of workplace democracy is unmistakable: it challenges the institutional concentration of economic power. From the perspective of ensepulcher, it interrupts the burial of alternatives by demonstrating that capitalist hierarchy is not the only possible way to organize productive life. What has been constructed historically can be transformed historically. EDUCATION: REPRODUCING THE MAUSOLEUM OR OPENING ITS DOORS The struggle over socialism cannot be separated from the struggle over education. Schools and universities are not institutions floating above the economic order. They are situated within social relations that shape their funding, purposes, curricula, labor arrangements, and definitions of success. Education can help reproduce the assumptions of the existing order, but it can also become a site for questioning and transforming them. When education is increasingly subordinated to market priorities, students are encouraged to understand themselves as human capital requiring continual investment, upgrading, and competitive positioning. Knowledge is valued according to its measurable economic return. Teachers are subjected to managerial regimes of performance measurement. Universities are pressed to behave like corporations, students are recast as consumers, and the purposes of learning are narrowed to employability, productivity, and institutional prestige. The problem is not that employment, practical knowledge, or economic security are unimportant. They matter profoundly. The problem arises when these concerns become the dominant measures of education's worth, displacing its democratic, ethical, intellectual, and emancipatory purposes. Here ensepulcher becomes especially useful as an analytical concept. The educational burial of possibility occurs when students are taught—explicitly or implicitly—that social arrangements are beyond their control; that poverty is principally a personal failure; that competition is the natural condition of human existence; that the market is the ultimate arbiter of value; and that imagining a radically different society is naïve or irresponsible. The process is successful when the boundaries of what can be imagined come to resemble the boundaries of what can be done. Mausolocracy describes the larger institutional order that protects concentrated power. Ensepulcher describes the educational and ideological practices through which that order reproduces itself, including the narrowing of knowledge, the marginalization of dissent, and the conversion of historically contingent social arrangements into seemingly permanent truths. Yet education is never simply a machine for reproducing domination. Its contradictions can open spaces for critical inquiry, collective reflection, and democratic struggle. Teachers and students can examine how economic power shapes the conditions of learning, whose knowledge is legitimized, whose histories are excluded, and what forms of human possibility are rendered invisible. FREIRE, REVOLUTIONARY CRITICAL PEDAGOGY, AND THE STRUGGLE AGAINST ENSEPULCHER Paulo Freire's critique of the banking model of education remains indispensable here. In Pedagogy of the Oppressed, Freire challenges an educational relationship in which teachers deposit knowledge into passive students, treating learners as receptacles rather than as subjects capable of interpreting and transforming their world. Against this model, he advances dialogical, problem-posing education grounded in critical reflection and action. Freire's contribution is not simply a more humane teaching technique. It is a challenge to relations of domination embedded in the production of knowledge. Students must be able to investigate the social conditions shaping their lives, recognize contradictions, and develop the capacity to act collectively upon them. Learning becomes inseparable from praxis: the dialectical relationship between reflection and action. But a critical pedagogy adequate to the present must also ask how educational institutions are situated within the wider organization of capitalist society. It must investigate ownership, class relations, the appropriation of surplus, and the ways capitalism intersects with racism, patriarchy, colonialism, and other structures of domination. It must examine not only what is taught but also who controls the institution, whose labor sustains it, which communities benefit from it, and whose needs remain subordinated. This is where my work on revolutionary critical pedagogy enters the argument. In my dialogue with Glenn Rikowski, Pedagogy for Revolution against Education for Capital , we addressed the relationship between education and the capitalist social relations within which it operates. That relationship cannot be adequately understood by treating educational inequality as a collection of isolated problems to be corrected while leaving the underlying organization of economic power untouched. A revolutionary critical pedagogy does not simply ask how education can help individuals succeed within the existing order. It asks how education can contribute to collective struggles capable of transforming the conditions that produce inequality in the first place. It seeks to make visible the social relations hidden behind apparently neutral arrangements, while developing the intellectual and political capacities necessary for collective agency. In this sense, revolutionary critical pedagogy contests ensepulcher directly. It brings buried possibilities back into public consciousness. It asks students to consider why workplaces are organized hierarchically, why some people command the labor of others, why productive abundance coexists with deprivation, and why decisions affecting millions are often made without meaningful democratic participation by those most affected. It does not promise that critical awareness automatically produces social transformation. Nor does it reduce education to political indoctrination. Its purpose is to make rigorous inquiry, historical understanding, ethical deliberation, and collective action possible—so that existing arrangements can be examined rather than simply accepted. A socialist educational vision would therefore require more than changing classroom content. It would also require confronting the material conditions of education: unequal access to resources, the exploitation and precarity of educational labor, the privatization of public goods, and the growing influence of corporate interests over institutional priorities. Emancipatory teaching cannot substitute for the transformation of unjust material conditions. But without critical education, those conditions are more likely to be reproduced as unquestioned common sense. FROM REVOLUTIONARY TO PROPHETIC CRITICAL PEDAGOGY My subsequent work with Petar Jandrić on revolutionary critical pedagogy and liberation theology extends this argument into an explicitly ethical and spiritual register. In From Liberation to Salvation: Revolutionary Critical Pedagogy Meets Liberation Theology , we explored the relationship between Marxist critique, liberation theology, solidarity with the oppressed, and the possibility of a transformed social order. Liberation theology insists that the suffering of the poor cannot be treated as an incidental cost of social progress or as a matter of private charity alone. It demands that the structures producing suffering be confronted. Its ethical challenge is inseparable from a material critique of the institutions that organize wealth, power, and exclusion. In this respect, it enters into a profound conversation with revolutionary critical pedagogy: both insist that the denunciation of injustice must be joined to practices that make liberation possible. This connection informs what I call prophetic critical pedagogy. The prophetic is not a prediction that history will automatically deliver a just society. It is a refusal to accept the present as the final horizon of human possibility. It joins the denunciation of oppressive realities to the annunciation of a more humane future, while recognizing that such a future must be created through struggle, solidarity, ethical commitment, and collective action. The distinction matters. Revolutionary critical pedagogy investigates and challenges the material and ideological relations that reproduce domination. Prophetic critical pedagogy carries that critique into a horizon of moral responsibility: it asks what kind of world we are obligated to struggle toward, whose suffering demands our attention, and what forms of solidarity are required if human dignity is to mean more than an abstract declaration. Liberation theology deepens this challenge by placing the lives of the poor and oppressed at the center of moral and political judgment. It contests the idolatry of money and the treatment of accumulation as an unquestionable social good. It insists that economic arrangements must be judged by their consequences for human beings, especially those whose labor and suffering are routinely rendered invisible. This is why the question of socialism cannot be confined to economic efficiency or institutional design. It is also a question of the kind of society we are willing to build, the forms of suffering we are willing to tolerate, and the responsibilities we recognize toward one another. A society may possess extraordinary productive capacity and still fail morally if that capacity is organized to preserve privilege while leaving people without the conditions necessary to live with dignity. SOCIALISM AS THE DEMOCRATIZATION OF POSSIBILITY Socialism must, of course, be approached critically rather than idealized. Its name alone does not guarantee democracy, justice, or freedom. Historical projects claiming socialist legitimacy have sometimes concentrated authority in the state, suppressed dissent, or preserved hierarchical workplace relations. These failures must be confronted honestly. Socialism worthy of the name must be judged by the actual democratic power it enables people to exercise, the freedoms it protects, and its capacity to meet human needs without reproducing new forms of domination. Wolff's emphasis on workplace democracy offers one important criterion: people should not be excluded from decisions that govern their working lives and determine what happens to the value they collectively create. Freire offers another: education should cultivate the capacity to read the world critically rather than merely adapt to it. Revolutionary critical pedagogy asks how these capacities can contribute to transforming the social relations that reproduce exploitation. Prophetic critical pedagogy asks what ethical commitments should guide that transformation and whose liberation must remain at its center. Together, these approaches help clarify the analytical relationship between mausolocracy and ensepulcher. Mausolocracy names the architecture of entrenched power; ensepulcher names the active burial of alternatives that helps sustain it. Revolutionary critical pedagogy investigates and contests the material and ideological mechanisms of that reproduction. Prophetic critical pedagogy connects such critique to a moral horizon of solidarity, liberation, and human possibility. The task, then, is not simply to make capitalism more tolerable while leaving its central relations of power intact. It is to democratize the institutions through which social life is organized, to expand the capacity of people to shape the conditions of their existence, and to reclaim education as a practice through which we learn to understand and transform the world we share. Socialism matters because democracy should not end where economic power begins. It matters because the people who collectively produce society's wealth should have a meaningful voice in determining how that wealth is used. It matters because education should do more than prepare people to occupy predetermined positions within an unequal order: it should help them understand why that order exists and how it might be changed. The mausoleum of capital is not invulnerable. Its apparent permanence depends upon institutions, practices, and beliefs that are historically made and therefore open to historical struggle. Ensepulcher is never complete, because the possibilities it seeks to bury can be recovered through critical thought, collective action, and solidarity. The purpose of revolutionary and prophetic critical pedagogy is not to decorate that mausoleum with the language of justice. It is to help dismantle the conditions that make it possible—and to participate in building a world in which the freedom and flourishing of each become inseparable from the freedom and flourishing of all.
